theory.intro: The word 'rate' describes how quickly a quantity is changing, and the same 'increasing/decreasing at an increasing/decreasing rate' language used for distance–time graphs works for any quantity that changes over time — a population, a temperature, a water level, or a crowd size. A straight line changes at a constant rate; a curve changes at a rate that is itself increasing or decreasing.
facts: A **straight** line changes at a **constant rate** — its steepness never changes.
A curve that is rising and getting **steeper** is **increasing at an increasing rate**; a curve that is rising but getting **flatter** is **increasing at a decreasing rate**.
A curve that is falling and getting **steeper** is **decreasing at an increasing rate**; a curve that is falling but getting **flatter** is **decreasing at a decreasing rate**.
The rate description always refers to how the **steepness** is changing, not to the value of the quantity itself — a quantity can be large and still be increasing at a decreasing rate.
steps: Decide whether the quantity is increasing, decreasing, or staying constant.
Decide whether the graph is straight (a constant rate) or curved.
If it is curved, decide whether it is getting steeper (an increasing rate) or flatter (a decreasing rate).
Combine the two decisions into the full phrase, e.g. 'increasing at a decreasing rate'.

foundation.solution_text:
The graph rises, so the population is increasing.
The curve gets steeper as time passes, so the population is increasing at an increasing rate.

The graph rises, so the crowd size is increasing.
The curve gets flatter as time passes, so the crowd size is increasing at a decreasing rate.

The graph falls, so the charge is decreasing.
The curve gets steeper as time passes, so the charge is decreasing at an increasing rate.

The graph falls, so the temperature is decreasing.
The curve gets flatter as time passes, so the temperature is decreasing at a decreasing rate.
The graph is a straight line, not a curve, so the fare is increasing at a constant rate — the steepness never changes.

The student is not correct.
The curve rises but gets flatter as time passes, not steeper, so the temperature is increasing at a decreasing rate, not an increasing rate.

development.solution_text:
Country X's curve gets steeper over time, so its population is increasing at an increasing rate — its growth is speeding up.
Country Y's curve gets flatter over time, so its population is increasing at a decreasing rate — its growth is levelling off.

Stage 1 (heating): the curve rises but gets flatter, so the temperature is increasing at a decreasing rate as it approaches the furnace's maximum.
Stage 2 (held at maximum): the line is flat, so the temperature stays constant.
Stage 3 (cooling): the curve falls and gets flatter, so the temperature is decreasing at a decreasing rate as it cools.

Graph Q shows revenue increasing at an increasing rate.
Graph P is a straight line, so it shows a constant rate, and Graph R gets flatter over time, so it shows a decreasing rate. Only Graph Q gets steeper over time, matching an increasing rate.

The student is not correct.
The curve gets steeper as time passes, not flatter, so the number of unsold tickets is decreasing at an increasing rate, not a decreasing rate — sales are speeding up, not slowing down, as the draw gets closer.

Battery X's curve gets steeper over time, so its charge is decreasing at an increasing rate — it is losing charge faster and faster.
Battery Y's curve gets flatter over time, so its charge is decreasing at a decreasing rate — it is losing charge more and more slowly.

Stage 1 (tap running): the line is straight, so the water height is increasing at a constant rate.
Stage 2 (someone in the bath): the line is flat, so the water height stays constant.
Stage 3 (draining): the curve falls and gets flatter, so the water height is decreasing at a decreasing rate.

mastery.solution_text:
Stage 1 (before school): the line is flat, so the number of cans stays constant — no one is buying.
Stage 2 (morning break): the line is straight and falling, so the number of cans decreases at a constant rate.
Stage 3 (lunchtime rush): the curve falls and gets steeper, so the number of cans decreases at an increasing rate as more people queue up.
Stage 4 (restock): the number of cans jumps straight up, which is not a rate at all — it is an instant change, not a gradual one.
Stage 5 (afternoon): the curve falls but gets flatter, so the number of cans decreases at a decreasing rate as sales taper off.

Country A's curve gets steeper over time, so its population is increasing at an increasing rate.
Country B's curve gets flatter over time, so its population is increasing at a decreasing rate.
Beyond the graphs shown, Country A is likely to have the larger population: a population that is still speeding up will keep growing quickly, while a population that is levelling off will grow only a little more, even though both reach a similar size by the end of the period shown.

The student has correctly identified that the level is decreasing, but has misdescribed the rate.
The curve gets steeper as time passes, not flatter, so the water level is decreasing at an increasing rate, not a decreasing rate — the reservoir is emptying faster and faster, not more and more slowly.
